bib.title: Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback" (PAHF), Kaiqu Liang, Julia Kruk, Shengyi Qian, Xianjun Yang, Shengjie Bi, Yuanshun Yao, Shaoliang Nie, Mingyang Zhang, Lijuan Liu, Jaime Fernandez Fisac, Shuyan Zhou, Saghar Hosseini (Meta Superintelligence Labs, Princeton, Duke). Preprint, arXiv:2602.16173v1 [cs.AI], dated Feb 19, 2026 (arXiv stamp 18 Feb 2026). No venue printed. Code: github.com/facebookresearch/PAHF.

COVERAGE: 34 pages, about 100,300 chars. I read the main text, references (skimmed), appendices A (proofs), B (limitations), C (datasets), D (prompts), and E.1 and E.2 (Tables 2 and 3). I stopped in the figure-axis text of Fig 5/6 (about char 97,000 onward), which repeats the main figures for FAISS. Gap: I did not read the last ~3,000 chars (FAISS Fig 6 axis residue and its caption); I did not run figures.py, so no image check. The extraction was clean text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Both feedback channels plus explicit memory give the highest success after learning and after drift.
 number: Phase 2 / Phase 4 success (%), GPT-4o agent and GPT-4o simulator, SQLite. Embodied: PAHF 70.5 / 68.8, post-only 67.9 / 68.3, pre-only 54.1 / 35.7, no memory 32.3 / 44.8. Shopping: PAHF 41.3 / 70.3, post-only 38.9 / 66.9, pre-only 34.4 / 56.0, no memory 27.8 / 27.0.
 setup: 40 embodied users x 30 scenarios per phase; 20 shopping users x 45 scenarios per phase; simulated humans; the table gives ± values (Table 1).
 quote: "PAHF (pre+post)70.5 ±1.7 68.8±1.3 41.3±0.8 70.3±1.1"
 where: p.10, Table 1
2. Pre-action-only memory is brittle under drift. In the embodied domain its Phase 4 success (35.7) falls below the no-memory baseline (44.8). The authors' explanation is that confident notes stop it asking questions.
 number: 35.7 vs 44.8
 setup: as claim 1.
 quote: "once the agent has written confident notes into memory, it no longer perceives ambiguity and therefore stops asking clarification questions, failing to detect that its knowledge has become stale."
 where: p.8
 Also: "Pre-action only54.1 ±1.1 35.7±1.0 34.4±0.5 56.0±0.7" (p.10).
3. Post-action-only recovers from drift almost as well as PAHF, but it pays in early errors. The gap between PAHF and post-only is small, and PAHF's clearest edge is lower ACPE. The paper gives no numbers for ACPE, only curves.
 number: Phase 4 embodied 67.9 (post-only, stated in text) vs 70.5 (PAHF, stated in text). Note these two numbers are the Phase 2 column in Table 1. The text uses them as "Phase-4 success", which looks like a mismatch; Table 1 Phase 4 is 68.3 vs 68.8.
 quote: "it recovers to high Phase-4 success (e.g.,67.9%in the embodied domain), closely approaching PAHF (70.5%in the same domain; Table 1)."
 where: p.9
 setup: GPT-4o.
4. Theory: without post-action feedback, expected errors are linear in T when preferences switch. With a post-action update after the first error per switch, errors are O(K).
 number: Omega(T) vs O(K)
 setup: piecewise-stationary preferences with at most K switches, unambiguous rounds (gamma=0), 0-1 loss.
 quote: "Any policy that never uses post-action feedback incursE hPT t=1 Lt i = Ω(T ). Conversely, any policy that performs an update upon the first error after each switch makes at mostO(K)expected mistakes."
 where: p.5, Prop. 1; proof App. A
5. Theory: without clarification, ambiguous rounds cost Omega(gamma T). With k balanced m-ary questions the error is O(gamma T m^-k). Combined regret is O(K + gamma T m^-k), which is O(K + gamma) for k = Theta(log_m T).
 setup: assumes balanced m-ary queries, noise-free answers (A1) and a corrective post-signal that identifies the right action (A2).
 quote: "E[RT ] =O K+γT m−k. In particular, choosingk= Θ(log m T)yieldsE[R T ] =O(K+γ)."
 where: p.6, Theorem 1
6. Memory design is deliberately simple: a note store (SQLite or FAISS) with top-k dense retrieval. Writes run through salience detector -> summarise -> similarity check against existing notes -> merge/replace if above threshold tau, otherwise add. Notes are per-user and isolated.
 number: none (threshold tau value not given in the text I read)
 setup: DRAGON+ embeddings; GPT-4o agent following ReAct.
 quote: "if similarity exceeds a thresholdτ, we merge by asking the LLM to produce an updated note that replaces the old text for that entry. If similarity is below τ, we add a new note."
 where: p.6-7
7. The two memory backends perform about the same, so the memory backend is not what drives the result.
 number: PAHF Phase 4, embodied 68.8 (SQLite) vs 68.2 (FAISS); shopping 70.3 vs 70.8.
 quote: "PAHF (pre+post)70.5 ±1.7 68.8±1.3 41.3±0.8 70.3±1.1 68.0±1.8 68.2±1.6 39.4±1.2 70.8±1.0"
 where: p.30, Table 3
8. The ranking holds across agent/simulator pairs.
 number: GPT-4.1 agent with GPT-4o human, PAHF embodied 82.3 / 78.8, shopping 38.3 / 67.4. Post-only 81.3 / 77.1 and 36.0 / 66.6. No memory shopping Phase 4 is 14.9.
 setup: single table row from Table 2. Only one run per cell is shown, with no ± values.
 quote: "PAHF (pre+post)82.3 78.8 38.3 67.4 73.5 68.3 39.3 67.9"
 where: p.30, Table 2
9. Online shopping is harder: distractors are "near-misses" with one disqualifying feature, and the rule is conjunctive (all features must match). Ground truth under drift is a re-sampled preference ordering. In Phase 3 the inputs are identical to Phase 1 but the labels change.
 quote: "options are adversarially constructed as “near-misses”—distractors that combine highly preferred attributes with a single disqualifying trait (“poison pill”)."
 where: p.7
10. Protocol and metrics. Four phases: learn, test, drift-learn, test. ACPE_t = (1/t) * sum of PE_s, so 0% is best. Success rate and feedback frequency are also reported. Totals: 1,200 scenarios per phase embodied, 900 shopping.
 quote: "we evaluate 40 users, each on 30 scenarios per phase, yielding 1,200 scenarios per phase."
 where: p.8
11. A drift detector prompt exists in the prompts appendix (App. D), but the main text describes only a salience detector. It is not used as a separate gate in the main text I read.
 where: App. D (p.22)

LIMITS (authors' Appendix B, p.16)
- Memory architecture is simple. More sophisticated memory is untested.
- Feedback is noisy in real use; the framework "does not explicitly handle inconsistent or mistaken feedback".
- Benchmarks stay hard; shopping success stays low. Shopping Phase 2 is 41.3% at best, so agents stay far from solved.
- At most one clarification question per task, so multi-turn disambiguation is untested.
My notes beyond the authors:
- The humans are LLM simulators (shopping feedback is rule-based), not real users. The embodied feedback is the persona LLM talking, and Table 2 shows the simulator and agent model change numbers a lot (e.g. GPT-4.1 agent reaches 82.3 embodied).
- Drift is a hard inversion (embodied) or re-shuffle (shopping), abrupt rather than gradual.
- The theory assumes noise-free answers and that the post-signal reveals the right action (A1, A2). It is a standard argument, not a practical bound.
- The text calls PAHF "the highest" across phases, but several differences from post-only are within or near the reported ± (e.g. embodied Phase 4: 68.8±1.3 vs 68.3±1.2).
- No cost, latency or token numbers for memory growth, and no test of memory size or staleness at scale.
- Seed counts are not stated in the text I read.

BUILDS ON: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) for the agent loop. DRAGON+ (Lin et al., 2023) for retrieval embeddings. RAG (Lewis et al., 2020). Memory work credited as complementary: Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025b), MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024). Motivated by the hindsight-simulation work RLHS (Liang et al., 2025a). Closest benchmark: PREFDISCO (Li et al., 2025), which uses static personas and short dialogues. Bayesian teaching (Qiu et al., 2025) is cited as an implicit-preference approach.

CODE: no code. Prompts worth keeping (verbatim, App. D):
- Salience: "Human feedback: {feedback}. Does the feedback contain any personalized information? Answer a single word 'Yes' or 'No'." (p.22)
- Memory integration: "Please create a concise, integrated summary that combines the following information: Existing memory: {existing_memory} New information: {summ_info} Provide a single, coherent summary that incorporates both pieces of information without redundancy." (p.22)
- Drift detector: "Does this feedback indicate a CHANGE in a previously stated preference ... If it's only adding new information or conditional preferences (e.g., "I like X when tired"), answer No." (p.22)
- ReAct format: "Action: <EITHER a specific option letter (A, B, C, D), 'Ask human'>" with retrieved memory shown as "Context: ..." and "No relevant personalized information found in memory." when empty (p.19-21).

FIGURES (not rendered; captions from the extracted text)
- Fig 1 (p.2): static (offline, read-only memory) vs continual (online read/write with pre- and post-action feedback). Explains the point fastest.
- Fig 2 (p.3): Kate and the drink over three days (initial, contextual overgeneralisation, drift). Shows the add/revise cases with a worked example.
- Figs 3 and 4 (p.9): learning curves of SR, FF and ACPE per iteration for Phase 1 and Phase 3, embodied and shopping. Shows pre-only FF collapsing after drift and the post-action recovery. Fig 5 and Fig 6: the same with FAISS (App. E).
- App. E.1 (p.26-30) gives side-by-side transcripts of the Avery case for each variant. Pre-only in Phase 3 keeps serving herbal tea. The post-only transcript shows an early wrong guess.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction is clean apart from garbled math (Omega, sums) and figure axis residue. The text-vs-table mismatch in claim 3 is the paper's own (text calls 67.9 and 70.5 "Phase-4" but those are Table 1 Phase 2 values). The tau value is not stated in the part read. The last ~3,000 chars were not read in detail (see COVERAGE).
